summary: Most VFR-into-IMC accidents follow poor weather decisions, pressure to press on, and no instrument skills. Plan a minimum safe altitude (add 500 or 1,000 ft to the MEF), avoid flight below 1,500 ft AGL en route, and decide early to turn back. If you enter IMC, fly the attitude indicator, make a gentle rate 1 turn of no more than 20° bank through 180°, call ATC and make a MAYDAY. Built from CAA Safety Sense Leaflet 33.
src: Safety Sense Leaflet 33: VFR Flight into IMC
sections: Causes of VFR into IMC
Complex or uncertain forecasts, or only checking departure and destination weather
Weather deteriorating on the day, and pressure to continue (get-there-itis)
Distraction from navigation or radio
No instrument qualification: instrument flying is a separate perishable skill
Spatial disorientation types
Visual: false horizon from sloping cloud
Vestibular: the leans, feeling banked the wrong way
Somatogravic: acceleration feels like a pitch-up
Coriolis: head movement in a prolonged turn gives false rotation
Inversion: abrupt level-off feels like tumbling
Planning to avoid IMC
Watch weather for days beforehand and review METARs, TAFs and the F215 chart. Account for elevation differences
Red flags: widespread PROB30, big time windows for change, unclear early-morning data
Warm fronts: low cloud and poor visibility. Cold fronts: showers with unpredictable cloud. Persistent high pressure: haze and unclear horizon
Set a minimum safe altitude: add 500 ft or 1,000 ft to the Maximum Elevation Figure (MEF) for each quadrangle
En-route flight below 1,500 ft AGL is not recommended
Have a Plan B, identify diversion aerodromes, and brief passengers that weather may change the plan. Do not take off just to have a look
VFR on top
VMC above cloud without sight of the surface
Risks: no hole at the destination to get down, and an emergency above cloud
Class G at or below 3,000 ft AMSL (or 1,000 ft above terrain, whichever is higher): remain in sight of the surface
Above 3,000 ft AMSL: 5 km visibility, 1,500 m horizontal and 1,000 ft vertical from cloud
In-flight decisions and warning signs
Use planned decision points and look ahead and to the sides
Warning signs: scraps of cloud passing close, intermittent loss of horizon, a warm front sky closing the gaps, haze or rain fading the horizon
High risk at night, over sea and over featureless terrain
Start recovery when you recognise the risk, not after you enter cloud
Never descend below MSA in IMC. If weather closes in on all sides, consider a precautionary field landing
If you enter IMC
Priorities: Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Trust the instruments, focus on the attitude indicator, make small inputs and trim
If control is difficult, hold straight and level and avoid power changes and turns
Turn 180° once stable, toward where you believe VMC lies
The 180° turn
Note the target heading, choose a direction, and set a rate 1 turn with bank no more than 20°
Use a little back pressure to prevent descent and scan attitude, heading, airspeed and turn coordinator
Roll out near the target heading and hold it until visual references appear
No attitude indicator: use altimeter and turn and slip, keeping the altimeter steady
No heading indicator: rate 1 takes 2 minutes for 360°, so 1 minute for 180°. Do not trust the compass in the turn
Calling for help
Call ATC as soon as you have capacity, but fly the aircraft first
A MAYDAY is appropriate in VFR into IMC
Be honest that you are not IMC qualified. Best help: units with radar, or the D&D cell on 121.5 MHz
Landing below VFR minima is a last resort and a practised SRA can help

quiz.q: A sensible minimum safe altitude margin above the MEF is:
quiz.why: The leaflet notes common practice of adding 500 or 1,000 ft.

quiz.why: Rate 1 turn, no more than 20° bank, with a little back pressure.

quiz.q: Which illusion makes acceleration feel like a pitch-up?
quiz.why: Somatogravic illusion is caused by rapid acceleration.

quiz.q: Which call is appropriate when you inadvertently enter IMC without a rating?
quiz.why: The leaflet advises a MAYDAY call in a VFR-into-IMC situation.
